guidance: A starting point for established trees, not a prescription: it assumes ten US gallons per inch of trunk diameter applied slowly inside the drip line and does not model species, soil, weather or drainage.
method: The rule of thumb used here is ten US gallons of water for every inch of trunk diameter, measured at knee height, applied slowly within the drip line. A diameter in centimetres is divided by 2.54 to give inches and the soak volume is ten times that figure, so the rule is about 3.79 litres per inch, or roughly 15 litres per centimetre of trunk diameter. The page reports the soak volume in litres and US gallons, multiplies by the number of soaks per week for a weekly total, and divides by the hose flow you enter for the time it takes to apply. Bucket and watering-can counts round up, because a part-filled container is still one to carry. The rule is a starting point rather than a prescription: it is written for established trees, newly planted trees want smaller and more frequent soakings, soil texture changes how far a given volume spreads, and hot windy weather raises demand, so check the soil with a trowel before watering again. Wetting to about 12 inches, splitting a soak into two passes when water starts to pool, and keeping the water off the trunk are application details the arithmetic does not model. Everything runs in your browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Arbor Day Foundation, How to Properly Water Your Trees: the rule of thumb for established trees is 10 gallons of water for each inch of the tree’s diameter, measured at knee height
Denver Water, Tree Care Guide: apply water slowly within the drip line to a depth of 12 inches, and in dry winter periods use 10 gallons for each inch of the tree’s diameter
